The front desk as the operational hub of the lodging property, reporting inside the rooms division to the front office manager

Room status terminology used to coordinate the front desk with housekeeping (occupied, vacant and ready, on-change, stayover, due-out, out-of-order, no-show, skipper)

claims.claim: Front-office work is organized around the guest cycle, conventionally taught as four stages: pre-arrival (the reservation), arrival (registration/check-in and room assignment), occupancy (guest services and charge postings to the account), and departure (check-out and settlement). Some texts add a fifth post-departure stage for guest-history follow-up.

The front office is the operational hub of a lodging property. It sits inside the rooms division, is directed by the front office manager who controls room availability and the day-to-day functions of the desk, and is where guests have most of their direct transactions with the hotel.

Front desk agents / hotel, motel, and resort desk clerks greet and register guests and assign rooms, make and confirm reservations, post charges (rooms, food, telephone, and other services) to guest accounts, keep records of room availability and guests' accounts, compute bills and collect payment, and review accounts and charges with guests at check-out.
The guest's experience with a property typically begins at the reservation, which creates the guest record before arrival; reservations agents also book amenities and activities beyond the room.

Reservations differ by the level of commitment between guest and hotel. A non-guaranteed reservation holds the room only until a cutoff (commonly 6 p.m. on the arrival date, the '6pm hold'), after which the room may be released; a guaranteed reservation is secured by an advance deposit or credit-card guarantee so the room is held and the guest is liable for a no-show under the hotel's policy.
The guest folio is the running account of all charges and credits posted to a guest's stay; charges accumulate on it throughout occupancy and are settled at departure.

The night audit is the daily control process that reconciles guest accounts and departmental financial activity: it completes outstanding postings, posts room and tax charges to occupied rooms, verifies no-show reservations, checks rate variances, balances departmental revenue (food and beverage, telephone, etc.) against the front-office ledger, prepares management reports, and then runs the end-of-day process that rolls the business date, closing the hotel's financial day.

Room status terminology lets the front desk and housekeeping coordinate which rooms can be sold: occupied, vacant and ready, on-change (departed but not yet cleaned), stayover (guest remaining another night), due-out (expected to depart after today's check-out time), out-of-order (unsellable), no-show (a reservation that never arrived), and skipper (a guest who left without settling).

Occupancy percentage, an operational statistic the night audit reports for the manager's desk report, equals rooms sold divided by rooms available, expressed as a percentage; properties may compute the denominator on total rooms or on rooms available for sale (excluding out-of-order rooms).

In the United States, the median annual wage for lodging managers was $68,130 in May 2024 (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook); front-desk managers within that group coordinate reservations and room assignments and direct front-desk staff.

positions: Most front-office texts describe four stages: pre-arrival, arrival, occupancy, departure.
Some texts add a fifth, post-departure, to capture guest-history and follow-up marketing.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the four operational stages and notes the optional fifth stage as a common variant, so readers recognize either presentation.

positions: Rooms available = total rooms in the property.
Rooms available = rooms available for sale, i.e., total rooms minus out-of-order rooms.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The worked example shows both computations and states that the convention varies by property, so a reader is not misled into treating one as universal.
